First weeks feel disorienting for almost everyone — that's not a sign you're unprepared, it's just what novelty feels like. A few things worth holding onto:

**You're not expected to be useful yet.** Managers budget weeks or months for ramp-up. Your job right now is to learn, not to perform. Asking questions signals engagement, not incompetence — and there's a window early on where "sorry, I'm still new" is a perfectly good reason to ask anything.

**Take notes obsessively.** Names, acronyms, who owns what, how to access things. You'll forget more than you expect, and re-asking the same question in week six is more awkward than asking three times in week one.

**Prioritize people over tasks.** Learning who to go to for what will help you more than any single deliverable. Accept lunch invitations. Ask colleagues about their work — most people enjoy explaining it.

**Expect to feel stupid.** You've moved from knowing your old job well to knowing nothing. That contrast is uncomfortable, but it's temporary and universal.

**Be patient with the timeline.** Most people say things click around the two- or three-month mark. If week one feels rough, that's not data about whether you'll succeed.

Finally: they chose you. They saw enough to bet on you. Let that carry some weight against the doubt.

**Review: Anker Soundcore Space Q45 — Solid Value, Minor Compromises**

★★★★☆ (4/5)

I've been using these for about three months as my daily commuter headphones, and they've largely earned their $130 price tag.

**Sound:** Out of the box, the bass is heavy-handed — fine for hip-hop and electronic, muddy for acoustic tracks. Thankfully the app's EQ is genuinely useful; dialing the low end back a few decibels opened up the mids considerably. Detail retrieval won't threaten headphones twice the price, but nothing here sounds broken or cheap.

**Noise cancelling:** Impressive for the money. It flattens airplane drone and HVAC rumble almost completely. Human voices still cut through, so don't expect open-office silence.

**Comfort and build:** Lightweight with generous memory foam padding. I wore them for a five-hour flight without pain, though my ears got warm around hour three. The plastic hinges feel like the eventual failure point.

**Battery:** Outstanding. I charge roughly once every two weeks with ANC on, which is genuinely liberating.

**Gripes:** The touch controls register accidental swipes when adjusting fit, multipoint pairing occasionally drops my laptop, and the carrying case is bulkier than necessary.

**Verdict:** Not audiophile gear, but a well-rounded, low-risk purchase. If you want great battery life and competent ANC without spending $350, these deliver.

**On Solitude and Loneliness**

They wear the same face, at first. Both involve an empty room, an unanswered phone, a meal eaten without conversation. But anyone who has known them both can tell you they are not relatives so much as strangers who happen to dress alike.

Loneliness is a hunger. It is the ache of a door that will not open, the sense that something owed to you has been withheld. In loneliness, the self becomes unbearably loud—you circle your own thoughts, checking and rechecking whether you are wanted. Time thickens. The silence is not empty but crowded with the people who are not there.

Solitude is different. Solitude is a room you have chosen to enter, and the door is unlocked from the inside. In it, the self quiets rather than clamors. You notice the way afternoon light moves across the floor. You have the peculiar experience of thinking a thought all the way to its end, without interruption, without performing it for anyone. Solitude is not the absence of others so much as the presence of yourself.

What separates them, I think, is consent—and something like trust. Solitude requires the quiet confidence that you will be met again, that the world has not forgotten your name. Loneliness is what solitude becomes when that confidence fails.

Which suggests something hopeful, and something demanding. The same hours can be either one. What determines it is not the emptiness of the room but the state of the person sitting in it—and that, unlike the room, can be tended.

**Why coffee tastes bitter**

Bitterness is a chemical alarm system. Humans have about 25 different bitter taste receptors (called TAS2Rs) on the tongue, which likely evolved to warn us about toxic plant alkaloids. Coffee happens to be full of compounds that trip these sensors.

Caffeine is the famous suspect, but it accounts for only around 10–15% of coffee's bitterness. The bigger contributors are created during roasting. Green coffee beans are rich in chlorogenic acids—relatively mild-tasting antioxidants. Heat breaks these down into chlorogenic acid lactones, which taste pleasantly bitter, and, with more intense roasting, into phenylindanes, which are harsher and linger unpleasantly. This is why dark roasts taste more aggressively bitter than light ones, despite containing slightly *less* caffeine. Roasting also produces melanoidins, large brown polymers that add body along with a bitter edge.

Brewing matters too. Bitter compounds are larger and slower to dissolve than the fruity acids and sugars, so they emerge late in extraction. Water that's too hot, grounds that are too fine, or steeping that runs too long pulls out excess bitterness—that's "over-extraction."

A little bitterness is desirable: it provides structure and depth, much like hops in beer. We simply learn, through caffeine's rewarding effects, to enjoy a sensation we're born to distrust.

**The Quiet Rearrangement**

No one held a ribbon-cutting for it. There was no bond measure, no master plan, no mayor's press conference. But over the past five years, remote work has redrawn our cities more thoroughly than a decade of zoning fights ever could.

Start with the obvious: downtowns built to absorb a weekday tide now sit half-drained. The sandwich shop that survived on the 12:30 rush is gone. The parking garage charges less. The commuter rail runs emptier trains at 8 a.m. and, curiously, fuller ones on Saturday afternoons.

But the more interesting story is happening three miles out. Neighborhoods that were once dormitories — places people slept and left — have become places people inhabit at 11 a.m. on a Tuesday. Coffee shops added outlets and, in some cases, a second location. Parks filled with adults in the middle of the day, an odd sight in 2018. Local hardware stores, dry cleaners, and daycares found themselves serving a customer base that no longer disappears at dawn.

This isn't uniformly good. Tax bases built on office towers are wobbling. Housing pressure has migrated outward, pushing prices into towns that never asked for it. Downtown vacancy is a real problem requiring real conversion policy.

But the center of gravity has shifted from the office district to the neighborhood, quietly, without anyone's permission. Our policies haven't noticed yet. They should.

**How to Tie a Necktie (Four-in-Hand Knot)**

1. **Set up.** Pop your collar up and drape the tie around your neck. Place the wide end on your right side, hanging about 12 inches lower than the narrow end. Adjust so the narrow end sits roughly at your ribcage.

2. **Cross over.** Bring the wide end across the front of the narrow end, forming an X just below your collar.

3. **Wrap around.** Pass the wide end underneath the narrow end and back to the right, keeping the wrap snug.

4. **Cross again.** Bring the wide end across the front once more, left to right, so it now covers the wrap you just made.

5. **Up through the neck loop.** Push the wide end up underneath the loop around your neck, from below.

6. **Down through the knot.** Pull the wide end down through the front loop you just created.

7. **Tighten.** Hold the narrow end and gently slide the knot upward until it rests neatly against your collar.

8. **Finish.** Turn your collar down, straighten the knot, and check that the tip of the tie reaches your belt buckle. Adjust the length by untying and repeating if needed.

## HTTPS in a nutshell

When you type `https://example.com`, your browser opens a normal TCP connection (usually port 443), but before sending any HTTP data it performs a **TLS handshake**.

**1. Identity check.** The server sends its certificate: a public key plus a domain name, digitally signed by a Certificate Authority (CA). Your browser already trusts a set of CAs, so it verifies the signature, checks the domain matches, and checks the expiry date. This stops an attacker from impersonating `example.com` — they can't forge a CA signature.

**2. Key agreement.** Browser and server use asymmetric crypto (today, usually Elliptic-Curve Diffie–Hellman) to agree on a shared secret. Crucially, that secret is never sent over the wire — each side derives it — so an eavesdropper recording the traffic can't reconstruct it.

**3. Encrypted transport.** From then on, all HTTP traffic (URL path, headers, cookies, body, response) is encrypted with a fast symmetric cipher like AES-GCM, which also adds an authentication tag so any tampering is detected.

**What's still visible:** the server's IP address, the rough size and timing of traffic, and the hostname (via DNS and the TLS SNI field). The path, query string, and payload are not.

That's it: HTTPS gives you **authentication, confidentiality, and integrity** — but only for data in transit.

**4/**
The lesson: interest is not intent. The only validation that counts is evidence of existing spend — money, hours, or headcount already going toward the problem.

Most colleagues would rather explain something early than have you struggle silently. If you make a small mistake, treat it as useful information, correct it, and move on.

Set a few realistic goals for each day, such as learning one process, meeting a teammate, or completing a specific task. Small wins can make the environment feel more manageable. It may also help to prepare for the next morning before leaving, so you don’t carry every detail home with you.

When anxiety rises, pause and take a few slow breaths. Remind yourself that being new is a temporary stage, not a measure of your ability. You were hired because someone saw potential in you.

Finally, give yourself time. Confidence usually comes from repetition, not from feeling completely comfortable on day one. Be patient, stay open, and remember that you’re allowed to learn as you go.

Solitude and loneliness may look similar from the outside: one person, a quiet room, an empty evening. Yet inwardly, they are very different experiences.

Solitude is chosen, or at least welcomed. It creates space to think, rest, and listen to oneself without the demands of conversation or expectation. In solitude, silence can feel generous. A walk alone may become an opportunity to notice the changing light, sort through confused feelings, or simply exist without having to perform for anyone. Solitude can deepen our relationship with ourselves and, surprisingly, prepare us to connect more honestly with others.

Loneliness, by contrast, is not defined by being physically alone. It is the painful feeling of being unseen, misunderstood, or emotionally disconnected. A person can feel lonely in a crowded room, surrounded by friends, or even while sitting beside someone they love. Loneliness is less about the absence of people than about the absence of meaningful belonging. It makes silence feel like rejection rather than rest.

The difference, then, is not always external but emotional. Solitude gives us a sense of fullness; loneliness reminds us of an emptiness we wish someone else could share. Still, the two can overlap. A period of solitude may gradually become lonely, just as loneliness may lead us to seek restorative time alone.

Learning to recognize the difference is an important form of self-awareness. Solitude asks us to remain with ourselves; loneliness asks us to reach toward others. Both have something to teach us, but only one should be mistaken for contentment. Sometimes the wisest response to loneliness is not to endure it quietly, but to speak, call, visit, and allow oneself to be found.

Coffee tastes bitter because it contains several chemicals that activate our tongue’s bitter-taste receptors. The most famous is caffeine, but caffeine is only a small part of the effect. Roasting creates and transforms many other bitter compounds, including chlorogenic-acid lactones and, in very dark roasts, phenylindanes. These molecules are produced as heat breaks down sugars, acids, and other substances in the green coffee bean.

Bitterness is also influenced by how coffee is brewed. Hot water dissolves desirable flavors—such as sweetness, fruit-like acidity, and aromas—as well as bitter compounds. If the coffee is ground too finely, brewed too long, or exposed to excessively hot water, it can become “over-extracted,” pulling out more of the harsher compounds. Dark roasting and burnt grounds can intensify bitterness too. Conversely, under-extracted coffee may taste sour because acids are more noticeable than the later-extracting bitter compounds.

Our perception depends on more than chemistry. Genetics affect how sensitive someone is to bitterness, while milk, sugar, temperature, smell, and expectations change the experience. A moderate amount of bitterness can provide balance and complexity, much as it does in chocolate or beer. In coffee, it is usually accompanied by acidity, sweetness, body, and aroma. The goal of good roasting and brewing is not to eliminate bitterness, but to keep it from overwhelming the other flavors.

**The City After the Commute**

Remote work did not empty the city. It quietly rewired it.

Before 2020, urban life was organized around the office clock: trains filled at 8 a.m., coffee shops surged at noon, and downtown streets went silent after five. Now, that rhythm has loosened. The change is less dramatic than abandoned skyscrapers, but more profound. Cities are becoming places people use throughout the day—not merely places they travel to for work.

Neighborhood cafés have become unofficial offices. Libraries and parks are busier on weekdays. Parents can handle school pickup without surrendering an hour to traffic. A Tuesday afternoon now feels less like a dead zone and more like a normal part of civic life.

But this shift has exposed an uncomfortable weakness. Downtowns built around commuters are struggling to replace them. Restaurants that depended on office workers have closed, transit systems face financial pressure, and commercial towers risk becoming expensive monuments to an outdated routine. If cities respond by simply trying to lure workers back, they will miss the point.

The future city should not be designed around maximizing rush-hour foot traffic. It should be designed around residents: affordable housing, reliable broadband, lively public spaces, childcare, local shops, and transit that connects people to one another—not just to office towers.

Remote work has not killed cities. It has challenged them to become more than workplaces. The winners will be those that treat this disruption not as a temporary inconvenience, but as an invitation to build urban life around people’s time rather than employers’ schedules.

### How to Tie a Necktie: Four-in-Hand Knot

1. Stand in front of a mirror with your collar up and the tie around your neck. Place the wide end on your dominant-hand side, hanging about 8–12 inches lower than the narrow end.

2. Cross the wide end over the narrow end near your collar, forming an “X.”

3. Bring the wide end underneath the narrow end and toward the opposite side.

4. Cross the wide end over the front again, creating a horizontal band across the knot.

5. Lift the wide end upward behind the knot, passing it between the tie and your neck.

6. Pull the wide end down through the loop you created at the front of the knot.

7. Hold the narrow end and slide the knot upward toward your collar. Pull gently on the wide end to tighten it, but avoid making the knot too tight.

8. Center the knot beneath your collar and lower the collar points over it.

9. Adjust the tie so the tip of the wide end rests near the middle of your belt buckle or waistband. Tuck the narrow end into the loop on the back of the wide end.

10. Smooth the tie and straighten the knot for a neat, polished appearance.

HTTPS is HTTP sent through a secure connection created by **TLS (Transport Layer Security)**. It protects a web request in three main ways: confidentiality, integrity, and authentication.

When your browser connects to an HTTPS website, the server presents a **digital certificate**. The certificate contains the site’s domain name and a public key, and is signed by a trusted certificate authority (CA). Your browser checks that the certificate is valid and matches the domain, helping prevent an attacker from pretending to be the website.

Next, the browser and server perform a **TLS handshake**. They agree on encryption settings and use public-key cryptography to establish a shared, temporary **session key**. After that, the actual HTTP request and response—URLs, headers, cookies, and body data—are encrypted using fast symmetric encryption with this key.

HTTPS also adds integrity protection. Each encrypted message includes authentication data, so the browser can detect if someone changed it in transit.

A network observer can still see that you connected to a particular server, along with metadata such as timing and approximate traffic size. HTTPS generally hides the URL path, query parameters, request contents, cookies, and response contents, though some information such as the domain may be visible through DNS or connection metadata.

HTTPS protects data **between the browser and the HTTPS server**; it does not protect against a compromised server, malicious browser extensions, or malware on the device.

Coffee’s bitterness is primarily the result of chemistry, specifically the roasting process. 

Contrary to popular belief, caffeine only accounts for about 10% to 15% of coffee’s total bitterness. The real culprits are antioxidant compounds called **chlorogenic acid lactones** and **phenylindanes**.

Raw, green coffee beans aren't very bitter; they are packed with chlorogenic acids. When the beans are roasted, heat triggers the Maillard reaction (the same process that browns toast and sears steak). During light-to-medium roasts, these acids break down into *chlorogenic acid lactones*, which produce a mild, pleasant bitterness. However, as the roast gets darker, those lactones break down further into *phenylindanes*, which create a much harsher, more intense bitter flavor. This is why dark roasts taste significantly more bitter than light roasts.

Brewing also plays a role. If you use water that is too hot, grind the beans too finely, or let the water sit on the grounds too long ("over-extraction"), you pull out more of these harsh compounds. 

Interestingly, humans naturally evolved to dislike bitterness as a warning against toxic plants. But in coffee, a balanced level of bitterness creates the complex, rich flavor profile millions enjoy every morning.

HTTPS is standard HTTP traffic wrapped inside **TLS (Transport Layer Security)**. It prevents eavesdropping and tampering through a three-step process:

1. **Authentication:** When your browser connects to a server, the server sends its TLS Certificate. The browser validates this against trusted Certificate Authorities (CAs). This ensures you are talking to the actual server and not an attacker executing a Man-in-the-Middle (MitM) attack.
2. **Key Exchange (Asymmetric Encryption):** Next, the browser and server perform a "handshake." Using asymmetric cryptography (public and private key pairs), they securely negotiate a shared, temporary "session key" without ever sending the key directly over the wire.
3. **Data Transfer (Symmetric Encryption):** Once the session key exists on both sides, the connection switches to symmetric encryption (like AES). Symmetric encryption is computationally fast, making it ideal for encrypting actual HTTP requests and responses.

To tie a necktie, follow these steps:

1. Begin by facing a mirror and standing up straight. Place the tie around your neck with the wide end on your left side and the narrow end on your right side. The tie should be hanging down about 12 inches below your neck.

2. Cross the wide end over the narrow end, so that it forms an "X" shape.

3. Take the wide end and pass it behind the narrow end. Then, bring it up and over the knot, so that it forms a loop.

4. Bring the wide end down through the loop you just created in step 3.

5. You should now have a knot starting to form. Take the wide end and pass it behind the narrow end again.

6. Bring the wide end up and through the loop again, just like you did in step 3.

7. Pull the wide end gently to tighten the knot. Adjust the tie so it's centered and sits comfortably under your collar.

8. Tuck the narrow end of the tie into your shirt and you're done! Adjust the knot as needed to achieve a comfortable and symmetrical look.

When you make a web request, HTTPS (Hypertext Transfer Protocol Secure) ensures that the data exchanged between your browser and the server remains private. Here's how:

1. **Encryption**: HTTPS uses encryption to scramble the data being transmitted. This means that even if someone intercepts the data, they won't be able to read it.
2. **TLS Handshake**: When you visit a website, your browser initiates a TLS (Transport Layer Security) handshake with the server. This is a series of steps where the browser and server agree on a secret key to use for encryption.
3. **Certificate Verification**: During the TLS handshake, the server presents its digital certificate, which includes its public key and identity information. Your browser verifies the certificate to ensure it's talking to the genuine server.
4. **Symmetric Encryption**: Once the handshake is complete, the browser and server use the agreed-upon secret key to encrypt and decrypt the data being exchanged. This ensures that only the browser and server can read the data.

As a result, HTTPS keeps your web request private by encrypting the data and verifying the server's identity. This protects sensitive information, such as passwords and credit card numbers, from being intercepted by unauthorized parties.

Solitude and loneliness both involve being alone, yet they occupy opposite emotional landscapes. Solitude is a deliberate choice, a quiet room we enter willingly to hear our own thoughts. In it we read, walk, or simply sit, replenished rather than emptied. Time stretches generously; the self feels spacious and intact. Loneliness, by contrast, is an uninvited guest. It arrives when connection is desired but unavailable, turning empty hours into a hollow ache. Even a crowded room can feel desolate if no one truly sees us.

The distinction is one of agency and inner weather. Solitude is a sanctuary we construct; loneliness is a prison we did not choose. One invites reflection and creativity; the other breeds restlessness and self-doubt. A person can be physically isolated yet content in solitude, or surrounded by people yet painfully lonely. The difference lies not in the number of bodies nearby but in the quality of presence—our own and others’.

Learning to tell them apart is an act of self-knowledge. We can cultivate solitude as a renewable resource, scheduling it like any other essential practice. At the same time we can recognize loneliness as a signal, not a sentence, and reach toward genuine conversation or community. In honoring both states we become more fluent in our inner lives, able to rest in chosen quiet without fearing the unwanted silence that sometimes follows.

Coffee tastes bitter primarily because of chemical compounds extracted from roasted beans by hot water. Caffeine, an alkaloid, contributes a mild bitterness, but it is not the main source. Far more important are chlorogenic acids, which are plentiful in green beans. Roasting breaks them down into quinic acid, caffeic acid and related phenols that register as intensely bitter on the tongue.

The Maillard reaction—sugars reacting with amino acids under heat—also generates melanoidins, brown polymers that add roasted, bitter notes. Darker roasts produce more of these compounds, which is why they taste harsher. Over-extraction (too-hot water or too-long brew time) pulls extra bitter molecules from the grounds, amplifying the effect.

Humans detect these via TAS2R bitter-taste receptors, an evolutionary safeguard against toxins. In coffee the bitterness is usually balanced by acidity and sweetness, creating the drink’s characteristic complexity. Genetic differences in those receptors explain why some people find coffee far more bitter than others.

HTTPS wraps HTTP in TLS so a web request stays private even though it travels over the public internet.

Plain HTTP sends every byte—URL, headers, cookies, body—in the clear. Any router, ISP, or attacker on the path can read or alter it.

TLS first authenticates the server. The browser checks the server’s certificate, which is signed by a trusted CA and contains the server’s public key. This proves the client is talking to the real site, not an impostor (MITM).

Next comes a handshake. Using the public key (asymmetric crypto) the two sides negotiate a shared secret and agree on a symmetric cipher (usually AES-GCM). After that, all application data is encrypted with the fast symmetric key. Only the two endpoints hold that key, so intermediaries see only ciphertext.

TLS also adds integrity checks (AEAD). Any change to the encrypted bytes is detected and the connection is dropped.

DNS and the TCP handshake still happen in the clear, but the actual HTTP request and response—including the Host header and payload—remain confidential. The result is end-to-end privacy for the web request itself.

Coffee tastes bitter mainly because of chemical compounds created or concentrated during roasting, not just caffeine. While caffeine does add some bitterness, it’s only a small part of the story.

Green coffee beans contain chlorogenic acids, which are not very bitter. During roasting, heat breaks these down into chlorogenic acid lactones and phenylindanes. Phenylindanes, especially in darker roasts, are strongly bitter and give dark coffee its sharp, lingering bite. Roasting also produces other bitter-tasting molecules through browning reactions, similar to the way toast or grilled meat develops deep flavors.

Your tongue detects these compounds using specialized bitter taste receptors. Humans have many different bitter receptors, likely because bitterness often signals potential toxins in plants. Coffee triggers several of them at once, which is why its bitterness can feel complex and intense.

Brewing method matters too: longer brewing or very fine grinds extract more bitter compounds. But the biggest factor is roast level—light roasts taste brighter and more acidic, while dark roasts taste more bitter because roasting creates more of those bitter phenylindanes. So coffee’s bitterness is a natural result of heat transforming the bean’s chemistry.

Here is a simple step-by-step method for tying a classic Four-in-Hand knot.

1. Drape the tie around your neck with the wide end on your right, hanging about 12 inches lower than the narrow end.
2. Cross the wide end over the narrow end near your collar.
3. Bring the wide end underneath the narrow end and pull it to the right.
4. Cross the wide end over the front of the narrow end to the left.
5. Push the wide end up through the loop around your neck from underneath.
6. Tuck the wide end down through the front loop you just created.
7. Hold the narrow end and slide the knot up to your collar, tightening gently.
8. Adjust the dimple under the knot and center the tie.

With practice, this knot creates a neat, slightly asymmetrical look suitable for most shirts and occasions.

HTTPS keeps a web request private by layering TLS (Transport Layer Security) on top of HTTP over TCP. Privacy means that while an attacker can see the IP addresses and that a TLS connection is happening, they cannot read the actual request or response.

When a client connects to a server over HTTPS, they first perform a TLS handshake. The server presents a certificate proving its identity, signed by a trusted Certificate Authority. The client validates this certificate using the CA’s public key baked into the browser. The handshake then establishes a shared *session key* using asymmetric cryptography—often via Diffie-Hellman key exchange or RSA encryption. This session key is symmetric and known only to the client and server.

Once the handshake completes, all HTTP data—the request line, headers, and body—is encrypted with that symmetric key using a cipher like AES. Symmetric encryption is fast and efficient for bulk data. Additionally, each TLS record includes a message authentication code (MAC) to detect tampering, so an attacker cannot silently modify the encrypted request.

Thus, HTTPS ensures confidentiality: even if packets are sniffed on the network, the content is ciphertext that cannot be decrypted without the session key. The key itself is exchanged securely during the handshake, never transmitted in a readable form.

Behold, fellow citizens, for a plague has swept through our metropolises! Yet, unlike the fevers of old, this one brings no wailing in the streets, only a deafening quiet.

I speak, of course, of the Great Retreat. The exile of the clerk from his counting-house, lured not by duty but by the insidious comfort of his own hearth. Do not be fooled by the gentle hum of their infernal telegraphs! This is not progress; it is a rout.

Where once the thoroughfares thundered with the industry of a waking giant, now they stand as silent as a country churchyard at noon. The blacksmith of the modern age, the purveyor of sustenance for the working man, boards up his windows. The tavern, that great parliament of the people, stands hollow, for there are no throats to wet, no grievances to air.

We are witnessing the death of the Polis itself. Not by cannon fire, but by a thousand slippers shuffling to a thousand home offices. The clash of ideas, the friction of commerce, the very heat that forged our greatness—it all dissipates into the cold, empty air of the suburbs.

Rise up, I say! Demand the return of the herd! Or accept that we have voluntarily built our own mausoleums, brick by silent brick.
